query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled addition of 0.7 mol Al to a CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy will induce a phase transformation to a fine BCC structure that improves mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance in aerospace fastener applications.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy with primarily FCC structure, as typically processed without the Al addition.
generation.intervention: Add 0.7 mol Al in a controlled manner to the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed via standard casting and thermo-mechanical treatments and tested at room temperature under conditions representative of aerospace fastener service environments, including exposure to corrosive environments and mechanical loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase transformation from an FCC-dominated structure to a finer BCC-dominated microstructure, with accompanying grain refinement.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, due to its larger atomic radius and solid solution effects, promotes lattice distortions that trigger a phase transition to a BCC structure. This microstructural change enhances dislocation creep resistance and improves the formation of a more stable and protective oxide layer, thereby enhancing both mechanical durability and corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, the modified alloy should exhibit increased yield strength, improved resistance to room-temperature creep, and enhanced corrosion protection as evidenced by higher passivation behavior and lower corrosion current densities.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy without the 0.7 mol Al addition.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under processing conditions that allow for controlled alloying and phase transformation, and within the range of operational loads and corrosive exposures typical of aerospace fasteners. There remains a potential trade-off with ductility if the transformation is not finely controlled.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance between enhanced creep resistance/corrosion protection and any potential loss in ductility requires further validation. Optimal processing conditions to achieve the targeted fine BCC structure without adverse effects are still to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi-based HEA samples: one set with the standard composition (control) and one with an added 0.7 mol Al. Process both sets identically with controlled thermo-mechanical treatments. Perform microstructural characterization (e.g., XRD, electron microscopy) to confirm the presence of a fine BCC phase in the Al-added samples. Subject both sets to identical room-temperature creep tests, mechanical durability (yield strength, hardness) evaluations, and standardized corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution).
measurements: Phase identification and grain size via XRD and SEM/TEM
Creep strain and creep rate under a fixed load at room temperature
Mechanical properties (yield strength, hardness) from tensile/compression tests
Corrosion current density and passivation behavior from electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance, mechanical durability, and corrosion resistance (e.g., no lower corrosion current density and no evidence of a fine BCC microstructure) compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Polarization measurements were carried out in a standard three-electrode electrochemical cell at room temperature using a platinum counter electrode and a saturated silver chloride reference electrode. For Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.5 and Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.5Ag0.1, copper segregation along the grain boundaries was observed, which highly dissolved in the sulfuric acid solution and resulted in low corrosion resistance of the samples. Introducing Ag into Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.25 HEA led to the precipitation of a copper–silver eutectic structure, in which the copper regions were selectively dissolved in the sulfuric acid solution. The microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion properties of the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy were investigated under different conditions, including cold rolling and precipitation hardening treatment at various temperatures. The XRD patterns revealed that the alloy exhibited a single β phase in the solution-treated state. In contrast, the SIM transformation induced a β + α″ phase after cold rolling (50% and 75%), while heating at 350 °C for 15 min resulted in a β + α phase. Cold rolling significantly reduced the grain size of the β phase, while high-temperature precipitation hardening treatment led to larger grain sizes. Additionally, α precipitates were found in the ST sample after precipitation hardening treatment at room temperature for 30 days. After undergoing 75% cold rolling, the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy (CR75) exhibited a significant increase in yield strength, albeit with a slight increase in elastic modulus. Moreover, the corrosion resistance of the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy significantly increased after both the cold rolling and precipitation hardening treatments. Structural components used in high-temperature environments often fail due to high-temperature creep. Traditional creep tests, such as uniaxial tensile or compression tests, often require large sample sizes and long testing periods, which has limited the research on the creep properties of RHEAs. To overcome these limitations, the use of nanoindentation techniques for studying creep behavior offers an effective alternative. Nanoindentation is applying a small indentation load on the surface of the material to measure its mechanical properties, allowing for the assessment of creep properties at a very small scale. The advantages of this technique include the small size of samples required and short experimental periods. reading.lever: Introduce controlled 0.7 mol Al addition in a CoCrFeNi-based HEA to trigger a phase transformation toward a fine BCC structure.
reading.why: Al addition is shown to improve creep resistance and passivation behavior; applying it in aerospace fasteners should enhance combined mechanical durability, creep resistance, and corrosion protection.
